blocks.text: Paul instructs the Corinthians to gather a collection for believers in Jerusalem, using the same method he ordered in Galatia. Each person on the first day of the week should set aside money proportionate to their circumstances, avoiding collection when Paul himself arrives. This advance preparation prevents the high-pressure giving that can accompany a leader's physical presence. The Corinthians are to approve and endorse community representatives to carry their gift to Jerusalem, with Paul potentially accompanying them. This arrangement grounds carrier authority in local consent rather than unilateral appointment, and the use of letters from Paul anchors accountability across the network.

Paul writes from Ephesus, stating he will remain there until Pentecost. His reason combines attraction and obstacle: a great and effective opportunity for ministry alongside many adversaries opposing the work. This formulation—opportunity paired with opposition—shapes his timetable. He stays to sustain the work against resistance and to exploit the missional significance of the moment. The letter dates to approximately 53–55 CE, anchoring the composition in Paul's documented Ephesus ministry.

Paul expects Timothy to visit Corinth and instructs the community to ensure he has no reason to fear. Timothy performs the work of the Lord as Paul does—a formula legitimizing his labor as genuine ministry. The Corinthians share collective responsibility to welcome him peacefully and set him forward toward Paul. This charge makes the community corporately accountable for a delegate's physical and social safety. Paul also reports that he strongly urged Apollos to visit Corinth, but Apollos declined at that time, though he would travel when opportunity permitted. The text preserves a coworker's agency to refuse a requested itinerary without condemnation, showing Paul did not compel conformity and that Apollos retained independent judgment about his own movement.

Paul commands the Corinthians to watch, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, and be strong. Immediately after, he grounds all these directives in a single principle: let everything you do be done in love. The sequential structure makes love the controlling context for vigilance and strength. This pairing prevents the military and defensive metaphors (watch, stand fast, be strong) from justifying aggression, intimidation, or coercive enforcement divorced from affection. Spiritual strength expresses itself through love, not in opposition to it.

Paul names the household of Stephanas as the firstfruits of Achaia—likely the first household baptized or most prominent in the region—and notes they devoted themselves to service of the holy ones. He urges the Corinthians to be subject to such workers and to everyone who assists and labors in this way. The language acknowledges local household leadership while identifying these people as laborers whose work merits explicit recognition. Paul rejoices at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, who supplied what was lacking and refreshed both his spirit and the community's. He asks the Corinthians to acknowledge such people—treating their journey and service as acts worthy of corporate gratitude and reciprocal care, not silent delivery mechanisms.

Paul sends greetings from the assemblies of Asia and specifically from Aquila and Prisca and the assembly meeting in their house. Aquila and Prisca were mobile craft workers displaced from Rome by Claudian decree, who appear in Acts and Pauline correspondence at Corinth and Ephesus. Their mobility across Mediterranean ports shows translocal networks sustaining Christ communities. They hosted an assembly—evidence of a house-based gathering transcending formal civic or temple structures. The specific naming of their household assembly testifies to concrete locations where communities gathered and to the relational bonds connecting believers across trade routes and cities.
